newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wheat growers urge rethinking on bunt fungus.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wheat growers urge rethinking on bunt fungus.

text.p: The National Association of Wheat Growers (NAWG) has concluded its annual conference and called for karnal bunt fungus to be designated as a minor plant disease.

"In the interest of maintaining U.S. grain export markets and fairness to all domestic wheat producers, it is imperative that (the U.S. Department of Agriculture) and the wheat industry cooperate in an all-out effort to gain acceptance for designating karnal bunt as a minor plant disease," said a resolution passed by NAWG's board of directors.

NAWG's directors supported the establishment of a central office within the USDA to deal specifically with sanitary and phytosanitary issues. The directors also supported efforts to convene an international scientific forum to address wheat diseases.
Separately, the board elected Phil McLain of Statesville, North Carolina, president of NAWG. He will replace outgoing president Chuck Merja of Sun River, Montana.
Several countries temporarily halted imports U.S. wheat last March after karnal bunt was detected for the first time in the United States in Arizona durum wheat seed.

The USDA quarantined areas of the U.S. southwest where the fungus had been detected. A subsequent nationwide survey by the USDA concluded that the fungus spores had not spread into key wheat growing areas of the midwest.

Karnal bunt is not believed to be hazardous to human or animal health and it does not appear to have caused reductions in harvested quantities of wheat in the United States. It can, however, produce discoloured flour with an unpleasant smell or taste.

Many growers in the affected areas have complained bitterly about the USDA's strict response to the detection of karnal bunt. Some have also criticised the department for not doing enough to show other countries that karnal bunt is not as hazardous as originally feared.

But the USDA has maintained that its strict response was necessary to ensure confidence in the quality of U.S. wheat. Karnal bunt is considered a pest of quarantine significance by more than 30 nations with which the United States does business.
